books: The 1947 Sylhet referendum was held in the Sylhet district of the Assam Province of British India to decide whether the district would remain in undivided Assam and therefore within the post-independence Dominion of India, or leave Assam for East Bengal and consequently join the newly created Dominion of Pakistan. The referendum's turnout was in favour of joining the Pakistani union; however, the district's Karimganj subdivision remained within the Indian state of Assam.

Prior to the British arrival in the region in late eighteenth century, the Sylhet Sarkar was a part of the Bengal Subah of the Mughal Empire. Initially, the Company Raj incorporated Sylhet into its Bengal Presidency; however, 109 years later on 16 February 1874, Sylhet was made a part of the non-regulation Chief Commissioner's Province of Assam (North-East Frontier) in order to facilitate Assam's commercial development.

Baburi (Persian: بابری; Uzbek: Boburiy) was a boy in the camp bazaar of Andijan whom Babur describes in his memoir, the Baburnama, as the object of an infatuation in his youth. He is mentioned by name only in this one passage of the memoir, and nothing further is known about him.
The episode appears in the entry for 905 AH (1499–1500), immediately after Babur's account of his first marriage, to Ayisha Sultan Begum, in the month of Sha'ban (March 1500). Babur, then seventeen, writes that he found in himself "a strange inclination" for a boy in the camp bazaar "his very name, Baburi, fitting in", and that until then he "had had no inclination for any-one" and knew of love and desire neither by hearsay nor by experience. In the 2008 Uzbek edition of the text the boy is described as the son of the head of the camp bazaar.
Babur writes that he composed Persian couplets about his state and quoted a couplet of Muhammad Salih.

The Kanishka Stupa (Pashto: کانیشکا سټوپا; Urdu: کنشک اسٹوپ) was a monumental stupa established by King Kanishka of Kushan during the 2nd century CE in today's Shaji-ki-Dheri on the outskirts of Peshawar, Pakistan.
Considered among the tallest buildings in the ancient world, the stupa was built during the Kushan era to house Buddhist relics which were transferred to the U Khanti Hall at Mandalay Hill in Burma after their discovery.
According to Buddhists the building of the stupa was foretold by the Buddha:
"The Buddha, pointing to a small boy making a mud tope….[said] that on that spot Kanishka would erect a tope by his name." Vinaya sutra
The same story is repeated in a Khotanese scroll found at Dunhuang, which first described how Kanishka would arrive 400 years after the death of the Buddha. The account also describes how Kanishka came to raise his stupa:
"A desire thus arose in [Kanishka to build a vast stupa]….at that time the four world-regents learnt the mind of the king.
